indicators.note: 'in' puts the thing named before it inside the thing named after it, so one word is written round the other.

parts.note: a deed is the legal document that hands over a property or a title
to autograph a thing is to sign it

explanation.surface: Somebody adding their signature to a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Autograph' looks like a noun in the scene and is wanted as a verb. A deed is the crossword's default legal document, four letters and always available.
explanation.definitionFit: Something designed was worked out on paper before it existed, which is one particular way of having been created.

clue.text: Top of dragon boat is black

indicators.note: In a down clue the top of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: the first letter of DRAGON
the ark is the boat Noah built, and crosswords use it for any vessel

explanation.surface: The prow of a dragon boat, painted black.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface glues 'dragon' and 'boat' into one racing craft, which hides the fact that they are two separate instructions. Ark is the boat a setter reaches for first.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark names the absence of light, and in ordinary speech a dark sky and a black sky are the same sky.

indicators.note: Taking something partially means taking a part of it, so only a run of letters from inside the words is wanted.

parts.note: the letters run unbroken through haS A MOAt

explanation.surface: A country defending itself with a moat, like an oversized castle.
explanation.walkthrough: A nation with a moat is an odd enough picture to be worth a second look, and an awkward phrase is usually where a setter has buried letters. Samoa is a Pacific island state, so the surrounding water is nearly honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Samoa is an independent island country in the South Pacific, so it answers plainly to 'Nation'.

indicators.note: Something that is moving about is not settled anywhere, and letters that will not settle have to be put back in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: Finland furious about the way something ended.
explanation.walkthrough: Finland arrives looking like a fact about a country rather than seven letters to be broken up, and a proper noun is the last thing a solver thinks to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand finale is the big closing number of a show, put last precisely because it is the most impressive thing in it.

indicators.note: A dancer never holds a position, so the letters underneath will not stay in the order they are given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: A mother or father out on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' reads as part of the family scene — a parent catching a child — which is how a one-word definition at the front of a clue hides.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrap someone is to catch them in a trap, the verb built straight out of the noun.

parts.note: s = second, the unit of time
an automobile is a car

explanation.surface: A man called Mark and the second car he has owned.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is the verb 'is' in disguise, which is the commonest costume a link word wears. Reading 'Mark's second' as an ordinal is the trap; the clock is what is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the mark a wound leaves behind once the skin has healed over it.

indicators.note: Something out is out of its place, and letters out of place have to be resettled before they spell anything.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Washing spread on the rocks beside a Scottish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' looks like one phrasal verb, but only its second word does the shuffling and the first is fodder. A loch is a Scottish lake, and setters use the word for its letters far more often than for its water.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes is the everyday plural for the garments a person puts on, covering the whole wardrobe at once.

clue.text: Greek regularly put on glad rags for factory

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a steady interval, every second one, instead of all of them.
In a down clue one thing put on another sits above it, so the short piece goes in at the top and the rest hangs below.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of GREEK, taken at even spacing
glad rags are your finery, the best clothes you own

explanation.surface: A Greek who regularly turns up at the works in his best clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' can start from either end of a word, and here it starts from the second letter. Glad rags is British slang for the smart outfit kept for a night out.
explanation.definitionFit: A refinery is the plant where crude oil or raw sugar is processed into something saleable, so it is a factory of a particular trade.

clue.text: Dance and drink brown ale, initially

parts.note: rum is the spirit distilled from sugar cane

indicators.note: What happens initially happens first, so only the opening letter of each word named is wanted.

parts.note: the first letters of BROWN and ALE

explanation.surface: Dancing and drinking brown ale at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' sits at the end of the clue and reaches back over both of the words in front of it, not just the nearer one. Rum comes from the same islands as the dance, which is what holds the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance in a slow four beats, so 'Dance' names it by its class.

clue.text: Reprimand aristocrat suppressing expression of disgust

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down inside you, so whatever is suppressed is written within the word that does the suppressing.

parts.note: a toff is British slang for a rich, well-dressed upper-class man
ick is the noise people make at something revolting

explanation.surface: A lord swallowing his revulsion and keeping a straight face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suppressing' works on the surface as bottling up a feeling and in the wordplay as wrapping one word round another. 'Ick' is a grimace written down, and setters have taken to it gladly.
explanation.definitionFit: To tick someone off is British for giving them a telling-off, a reprimand well short of real punishment.

clue.text: Beginning to carry bar shoes for smart alec

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter of what follows is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of CARRY
a lever is a bar you push on to shift a weight
clogs are wooden-soled shoes

explanation.surface: Starting to carry a crowbar and a pair of shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to carry' reads as the start of an errand and means the start of a word. Clever clogs is a British nickname for someone who parades how much they know.
explanation.definitionFit: A clever clogs shows off their cleverness at every opportunity, which is exactly the person a smart alec is.

clue.text: Spooner's sentry arrived for poker, say

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two neighbouring words, so the two things named here trade their fronts.

parts.note: a sentry is a guard; it hands its hard G to the word after it and takes a C back
arrived = came; it gives up its C and takes the G in exchange

explanation.surface: A sentry turning up for the evening's hand, in a sentence the Reverend has mangled.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'guard came' and swap the noises at the front of the two words. William Spooner was an Oxford don whose habitual tongue-slips gave the device his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Poker is one card game among hundreds, and the 'say' marks it as an example of the class rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Layer of earth came down at last?

indicators.note: What comes at last comes at the end, so the final letter of each word named is the one wanted.

parts.note: eartH — last letter
camE — last letter
dowN — last letter

explanation.surface: A seam of soil that has finally subsided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Layer of earth' wants to be a geological stratum, but the join falls between the two words: 'Layer' defines and 'earth' starts the letter-hunt. The question mark flags a playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is the poultry-keeper's word for a bird kept for eggs rather than meat, which is the job this one does.

clue.text: Whistleblower playing well? I'm not sure

parts.note: a player in form is playing well, and the two words run together as one
er is the noise of hesitation someone makes while they think

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a player is on song, and not being certain about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark belongs to the surface's doubt and gives no instruction. 'In form' is British sports talk for a player whose game is going well just now.
explanation.definitionFit: An informer hands what they know about wrongdoing to the authorities, which is what blowing the whistle amounts to.

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so the word after it is written out backwards.
Something awful is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state are not in the order they ought to be.

parts.note: AN written backwards
anagram of PINK, 4 letters

explanation.surface: A hideous pink table linen sent back to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' and 'awful' each govern their own scrap of the clue and neither reaches into the other's. The pink is there to make a returned purchase sound plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: Napkin and serviette are the same square of cloth beside your plate; serviette is the word some British households prefer for it.

indicators.note: Shredding a thing cuts it into scraps that can be laid down in any order, so the letters that follow will not stay put.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Someone sly who has ruined a lace blouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like the crossword instruction to take a first letter and is only half of a garment. Seven letters of fodder spread across two ordinary words is the hardest sort of anagram to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A polecat is a wild member of the weasel family, and the name gets thrown at a person thought sly or treacherous.

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by mouth, so the word behind it is wanted for its sound and not its spelling.

parts.note: a geezer is British slang for a bloke, and in Britain the two words are said identically

explanation.surface: A man, by all accounts, sitting in a hot spring.
explanation.walkthrough: British pronunciation does the work here: the first syllable rhymes with 'please', which is exactly how the slang word for a man is said. North American speakers give it a long I and lose the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A geyser is a spring that throws up a jet of boiling water at intervals, a hot spring of the most theatrical kind.

definitions.meaning: to overcharge someone outrageously, stripping them the way a sheep is stripped
the zip-up top made of synthetic pile, named after the sheep's coat it imitates

explanation.surface: A swindle involving a jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from the sheep: one is its coat, the other is what shearing does to you. 'Rip off' has to be read as a verb, since the answer is one too.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to take their money as thoroughly as shears take wool; a fleece is also the pile-fabric jacket named after that wool.

indicators.note: Something found in a word is already sitting inside it, so the letters are read off exactly where they stand.

parts.note: the letters sit unbroken inside lOWLands

explanation.surface: A bird spotted somewhere in low-lying country.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads so naturally as habitat that the one long word never gets searched. Three-letter hidden answers are the easiest to bury, because a single word can hold them.
explanation.definitionFit: An owl is a night-hunting bird of prey, so 'Bird' names it by its class.

parts.note: the article taken as itself
l = large, the clothing size
to find a thing is to locate it

explanation.surface: Sharing out one big discovery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A large find' reads as a single noun phrase and is three separate pieces of wordplay. L for large is the label sewn into a shirt collar, which is where most solvers first met it.
explanation.definitionFit: To allocate something is to assign portions of it to different people, which is distributing it by another name.

definitions.meaning: to follow the marks something has left until you catch up with it, as police do with a missing person
the barely measurable quantity of a substance, too little to weigh but enough for an instrument to detect

explanation.surface: Hunting down a very small quantity of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses share an origin — a track left behind is a small remainder of what passed — so the clue reads as one idea rather than two. The first half is a verb and the second a noun, which is the only join the setter has hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: To trace a person is to follow their marks until you find them; a trace of a substance is the faintest quantity of it that still registers.

definitions.meaning: to put up with something unpleasant rather than protest about it
the marmalade-eating animal of Michael Bond's children's books, named after the London station where he was found

explanation.surface: Being asked to put up with Paddington.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' marks the second half as one of a class rather than a synonym, which is how a proper name can define a common noun. Paddington came from Peru and lodges with the Brown family in Notting Hill.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear a thing is to endure it; and Paddington is a bear, so naming him defines the species by one of its members.

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to close your grip round it, so the word doing the holding is written round the word it holds.

parts.note: mate is the everyday British word for a friend
Che Guevara, the Argentine who fought in the Cuban revolution, is the crossword's standard revolutionary

explanation.surface: A friend keeping hold of a rebel's blade.
explanation.walkthrough: Che Guevara lends his three letters to more crosswords than any other revolutionary, and a capital letter is never printed to warn you. 'Mate' turns up whenever a four-letter friend is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is the broad heavy blade used to hack through cane and undergrowth, a knife of the largest working sort.

parts.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis, written as a nought
to judge a thing is to rate it

explanation.surface: Being fond enough of a magistrate to stand up and speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' is the verb here, not the figure in the wig the surface offers. Love for nought comes from tennis scoring and is the commonest O in the crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal speech, usually a grand one, so the definition names the action rather than the speaker.

clue.text: Ceremony correct by the sounds of it

indicators.note: The phrase points at how a word is said rather than how it is spelt, so what goes in the grid is what the ear hears.

parts.note: correct = right, and the two words are identical in the mouth

explanation.surface: A ceremony that, from what people say, was done properly.
explanation.walkthrough: Right, rite, write and wright are all one noise in English, so the definition has to do the choosing. The sound is borrowed from an adjective even though what goes in the grid is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is the set form of words and actions performed on a solemn occasion, which is what a ceremony consists of.

clue.text: The setter can ultimately curse guys' fashion

parts.note: the setter is the person writing the clue, who calls himself me

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the very end, so the last letter of the word in front of it is the one taken.

parts.note: the last letter of CAN
to curse is to swear

explanation.surface: A crossword setter finally allowed to swear about what men are wearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The setter' is the crossword's way of saying 'me', and it appears whenever a clue seems to speak in the first person. The surface uses 'can' as a helping verb, which is the last place anyone looks for a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Menswear is the trade's name for the men's clothing department, so 'guys’ fashion' points at the same racks in slangier English.
